quote: - **Melnyk et al. (2015)** meta-analyzed ~600 resistance cost measurements and found costs in ~70% of cases with a mean relative fitness of 0.91–0.95 (5–9% cost). Their measurements are absolute fitness differences between isogenic resistant and sensitive strain pairs, while our +0.086 is a relative difference between AMR and non-AMR transposon knockouts within pooled libraries — these are different measurement scales.
heading: Literature Context

text: As reported for E. coli by Vanacker, Lenuzza & Rasigade (2023), plasmid-borne horizontally transferred resistance genes are less costly than chromosomal mutations. Applying that result to explain this report's modest pooled-knockout effect is an interpretation.
quote: - **Vanacker, Lenuzza & Rasigade (2023)** meta-analyzed fitness costs in *E. coli* and found that horizontally transferred resistance genes (plasmid-borne) are less costly than chromosomal mutations. This explains why our transposon-based cost estimate is modest — many FB AMR genes are likely acquired determinants (beta-lactamases, acetyltransferases) rather than costly target modifications.
heading: Literature Context

text: The report attributes metabolic efflux-pump costs from proton-motive-force drain and rapid compensation through metabolic rewiring in P. aeruginosa to Olivares Pacheco & Alvarez (2017); generalizing this mechanism to the cross-organism result is interpretive.
quote: - **Olivares Pacheco & Alvarez (2017)** showed that efflux pump costs in *P. aeruginosa* are metabolic (proton motive force drain) and rapidly compensated through metabolic rewiring. This explains why our efflux genes show the same modest cost as other mechanisms — compensation is a "general outcome."
heading: Literature Context

text: The report attributes to Levin, Perrot & Walker (2000) the finding that compensatory mutations arise faster than susceptibility reversion; its proposed irreducible-cost interpretation of +0.086 remains speculative.
quote: - **Levin, Perrot & Walker (2000)** demonstrated that compensatory mutations arise faster than reversion to susceptibility, predicting that organisms maintain resistance at reduced cost. Our +0.086 may represent the irreducible cost after compensatory evolution — the minimum overhead of expressing a functional protein that provides no benefit without antibiotics.
heading: Literature Context

text: Potential in-vivo benefits of resistance genes mean the in-vitro fitness-cost estimate may overstate ecological costs.
quote: - **Roux et al. (2015)** showed that resistance genes (particularly efflux pumps) can be beneficial in vivo by exporting host antimicrobials. This caveat applies: our in vitro cost measurement may overestimate the true ecological cost.
heading: Literature Context

text: All 25 organisms are lab-adapted; laboratory compensation may make measured costs lower than those in wild populations.
quote: 1. **Lab adaptation bias**: All 25 organisms are lab-adapted strains. Compensatory evolution during laboratory maintenance may have reduced measurable costs below what wild strains experience. This makes our positive result more convincing but may underestimate the true cost in natural populations.
